title: A theory of amorphous yielding that predicts the yield stress and whether failure is brittle or ductile

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a theory that starts from specified particle interactions and material preparation and predicts both the stress needed to sustain flow and how the material first gives way under loading. It would connect thermal-glass and jammed soft-particle regimes while distinguishing preparations that deform relatively homogeneously from those that undergo an abrupt stress drop, typically with deformation concentrated in a narrow shear band. The supplied scientific basis principally concerns frictionless spherical particles under simple shear.

Two connected prediction problems must remain distinct. Dynamic yield stress concerns the limiting stress associated with steady flow at very low imposed shear rate. Brittle or ductile yielding concerns the transient response as a prepared solid is first deformed. A theory could predict one without resolving the other. Likewise, a temporary stress maximum during startup does not by itself establish brittle failure: the report describes stress overshoots in otherwise homogeneous ductile yielding, whereas brittle yielding involves a macroscopic stress drop and typically localization.

The intended advance is predictive closure: the yield-stress scale and yielding outcome would follow from microscopic inputs and preparation, rather than being supplied through a fit to the target flow curve. This capability remains hypothetical in this record. The supplied review establishes the challenge as described in February 2024; it does not establish whether subsequent work has resolved it.

significance.text: Successful prediction would create a substantial connection between microscopic material physics and macroscopic mechanical response. It would explain how interactions and preparation determine whether an amorphous solid resists flow, deforms progressively, or releases stress abruptly through localized deformation. Covering both thermal-glass and jammed soft-particle regimes would bring together behaviors that existing approaches address with differing assumptions and restricted predictive reach.

The direct consequences of the proposed demonstration would be predictions of yield stress and yielding mode under specified loading, sample and observation conditions. Predicting the complete finite-rate flow curve would require an additional achievement. A general constitutive theory has an even broader task: predicting stress from preparation and deformation history. Solving the yielding problem would provide an important component of that theory without establishing every aspect of its response.

The comparison between brittle yielding and fracture is useful because an abrupt macroscopic stress drop is typically accompanied by deformation concentrated in a narrow band. It should not be read as an identity between shear localization and crack formation, or as evidence that every overshoot or shear band constitutes brittle fracture. The observable stress response and spatial deformation pattern must be assessed together.

Conditional application outlook: a validated theory could eventually help select preparations or processing conditions for glasses, pastes, emulsions, metallic glasses and coatings, and could inform models of geological materials. Those possibilities require evidence beyond the frictionless spherical-particle systems emphasized in the report. Broad industrial deployment and glass-composition design from chemistry would require additional microscopic modeling, material-specific validation and practical constraints; neither follows directly from predicting yield stress and localization in the proposed test systems.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central missing capability identified by Sollich's February 2024 report is a unified prediction of dynamic yield stress across both glass and jamming transitions. The difficulty includes predicting the stress scale and its variation with particle volume fraction and temperature. The reviewed approaches have different limitations: elastoplastic and shear-transformation-zone models generally take the yield-stress scale as an input, while mode-coupling, random-first-order and high-dimensional approaches offer restricted or not-yet-solved predictions. Their differing flow-curve predictions should not be collapsed into a claim that all fail for the same reason.

A second barrier is connecting preparation-dependent microscopic structure to collective failure. Simulations under athermal quasistatic shear show a ductile-to-brittle change, but the report leaves open its universality class, its behavior beyond that loading limit and its character in very large systems. Pronounced finite-size effects complicate extrapolation. Continuum arguments suggesting that finite stress overshoots generically generate shear-banding instabilities raise a further question: an apparently homogeneous response in a finite sample may not determine the large-system outcome.

The mathematical and computational barrier is also concrete. High-dimensional mean-field equations for steady shear had been derived, but the report states that they had resisted numerical solution and therefore had not yielded concrete steady-flow curves or yield-stress predictions. Existing finite-amplitude quasistatic results do not remove this steady-flow bottleneck.

Engineering synthesis: a usable predictive theory would need an operational description of preparation, a way to carry that information into stress and localization predictions, and calculations that remain tractable for the intended test systems. Its predictions would also need to state how loading rate, geometry, system size and thermal observation time affect the result. These are proposed requirements for making the capability testable, rather than additional achievements established by the supplied evidence.

current_state.text: The supplied assessment is grounded in Peter Sollich's report, Challenges in the rheology of glasses, prepared for the 29th Solvay Conference on Physics and available as arXiv:2401.16409. Its first submission was 29 January 2024 and version 2 was revised on 9 February 2024. The supplied materials identify it as a proceedings contribution available through arXiv; they do not establish a journal DOI or a subsequent publication history. Its account of unresolved problems should therefore be read as a dated assessment, not as a verified statement of the field on 1 November 2026.

By that assessment, high-dimensional mean-field equations for steady shear of soft particles existed, but numerical solutions needed for concrete flow-curve and yield-stress predictions were unavailable. The report distinguishes this limitation from existing results for finite-amplitude quasistatic deformation. Thus, formal equations and partial predictions had been achieved without the unified predictive closure proposed here.

Particle simulations had demonstrated preparation-dependent ductile and brittle responses under athermal quasistatic shear. This is a particular loading limit: thermal fluctuations are absent and deformation proceeds quasistatically. These findings establish meaningful phenomenology, but do not by themselves settle finite-rate behavior or the infinite-system limit. The report emphasizes pronounced finite-size effects and an unresolved universality class for the ductile-to-brittle transition.

Continuum-model arguments discussed in the report suggest that finite stress overshoots should generically produce shear-banding instabilities. This is a theoretical suggestion relevant to interpreting the large-system limit, rather than a demonstrated universal result for every material and loading condition. It also does not make an observed stress overshoot sufficient evidence of brittle failure in a particular sample.

Oscillatory yielding presents related, still unresolved questions. The report describes an absorbing-state character when the transition is approached from the fluidized side at large strain amplitude, and discusses connections with reversible–irreversible and random-organization transitions. Those connections constitute existing theoretical and phenomenological progress; the precise nature of oscillatory yielding and its relationship to the broader yielding problem remain questions in the February 2024 account.

The supplied review reports access to the full PDF text, while the retained arXiv landing page supplies identity, abstract and version metadata rather than the full scientific argument. Figure images were not inspected, and some text extracted from reproduced figures was garbled; the findings above rely on explicit prose. The alternative ar5iv rendering was not captured, so its proposed quotations were not independently checked there. No bounded search results establish developments after February 2024 through 1 November 2026. These limitations restrict freshness and figure-based interpretation without showing that the reported results are false.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: specify particle interactions and preparation before predicting the dynamic yield stress across test conditions spanning thermal-glass and jammed soft-particle regimes. Do not fit the target flow curve or insert its measured yield stress as an input. State any independently measured parameters and their uncertainties. Predictions should include particle simulations withheld from theory development, with coverage chosen to test transfer across regimes rather than only interpolation within a fitted example.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed demonstration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed failure-mode test: predict which preparations yield relatively homogeneously and which undergo abrupt, localized failure under specified loading. Compare stress histories with spatial strain measurements, including at least one laboratory system such as a colloidal glass or dense emulsion. Require the spatial evidence so that a startup stress overshoot is not mistaken for brittle failure. Define beforehand what observations will count as homogeneous yielding, localization and a macroscopic stress drop.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed failure-mode test

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirements: disclose preparation procedures, interactions or independently measured material parameters, geometry, boundaries, loading rates, system sizes and thermal observation times. Set quantitative prediction tolerances before evaluating the withheld cases, repeat tests across independent preparations, and make the theoretical calculations and comparison data reproducible. No numerical success threshold is supplied by the evidence, so tolerances must be proposed and justified for the intended application rather than presented as established standards.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed reproducibility requirements

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: vary rate and sample size sufficiently to identify where quasistatic or finite-size results cease to transfer, and report uncertainty near changes in yielding mode. A successful finite test set would establish demonstrated breadth within its tested materials and conditions. One laboratory system would provide bounded experimental validation, not universal coverage of amorphous solids. Complete finite-rate flow curves, oscillatory loading, frictional particles and chemically realistic materials would require separately stated demonstrations.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed practical boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: RHE-01, A constitutive closure that still works in a flow it was not fitted to, concerns transfer between flow conditions. RHE-02 supplies microscopic yielding physics that could become part of such a closure, while separately addressing steady-flow yield stress and startup failure. Predicting these quantities in simple shear would not establish RHE-01's transfer capability. Only roster titles were supplied for the other concepts, so these boundaries are provisional.

Roster-based synthesis: RHE-03, A continuum law for dense particulate flow from creep to inertia in an arbitrary shape, overlaps through dense-particle mechanics and the onset of flow. Its title emphasizes continuum behavior across flow regimes and geometry, whereas RHE-02 emphasizes yield-stress prediction and preparation-dependent failure. RHE-10, A constitutive law for magma that contains both crystals and bubbles, may share questions about yielding in complex mixtures, but its multiphase material scope requires physics and validation beyond the frictionless-particle basis here.

Roster-based synthesis: RHE-04, Inverse molecular design of nonlinear polymer-melt rheology, and RHE-11, A topology-based rheology of ring polymers, from pure melts to threaded states, also connect microscopic inputs with macroscopic response. Their stated targets concern molecular design and polymer topology, respectively. RHE-02's proposed yielding predictions neither solve those polymer problems nor establish chemistry-based inverse design.

Roster-based synthesis: RHE-05, A constitutive theory of active stress that can be inverted for a mechanical task, addresses activity-generated stress and task-directed inversion. RHE-06, Addressable solid–fluid switching that stays put without a sustaining field or settling particles, addresses controlled switching and persistence of the selected state. Both relate broadly to controlling mechanical behavior, but neither capability follows from predicting passive amorphous yielding.

Roster-based synthesis: RHE-07, The local three-dimensional stress in a flowing material, without assuming the constitutive law, concerns measurement rather than predictive closure. Such measurements could help test a yielding theory, while the proposed RHE-02 validation specifically requires spatial strain information to diagnose localization. Neither concept subsumes the other.

Roster-based synthesis: RHE-08, A predictive theory of elasto-inertial turbulence and of the drag-reduction ceiling, concerns a different collective flow phenomenon. RHE-09, Computing viscoelastic flow at the elasticity of real processing, concerns computational access to demanding viscoelastic conditions. They share the broader goal of predictive rheology, but success in either would not establish yield stress or brittle-versus-ductile failure from preparation, and RHE-02 would not establish their turbulence or processing capabilities.

change_log.change: Preserved RHE-02's identity and integrated microscopic prediction, steady-flow yield stress and preparation-dependent startup failure into a unified explanation.
change_log.reason: The research and review identify a coherent innovation while emphasizing that its two principal prediction tasks remain scientifically distinct.

change_log.change: Dated claims of unresolved capability to the February 2024 assessment and explicitly retained the absence of verified later developments.
change_log.reason: The supplied search record does not establish the field's state through 1 November 2026.

change_log.change: Bound the demonstrated technical basis principally to frictionless spherical particles under simple shear.
change_log.reason: The report does not establish equivalent predictive coverage for metallic glasses, coatings, frictional materials or geological systems.

change_log.change: Distinguished input stress scales, restricted predictions and unsolved equations across the reviewed theoretical approaches.
change_log.reason: The original wording grouped different limitations too broadly and obscured existing partial progress.

change_log.change: Separated yield-stress and yielding-mode prediction from complete finite-rate flow-curve prediction and general constitutive closure.
change_log.reason: The proposed completion tests do not establish those broader capabilities.

change_log.change: Preserved the fracture analogy while explaining why an overshoot alone does not diagnose brittle failure.
change_log.reason: The report permits overshoots during homogeneous ductile yielding and describes localization as typical of brittle yielding rather than universally identical to fracture.

change_log.change: Qualified continuum localization arguments and retained finite-size, finite-rate and oscillatory-yielding distinctions.
change_log.reason: Theoretical suggestions and unresolved extrapolations should not be presented as universal demonstrated outcomes.

change_log.change: Recast industrial applications and composition design as conditional possibilities requiring further physics and validation.
change_log.reason: The evidence does not support blanket statements about modeling practice or the claimed specific necessity of an equilibrium-liquid molecular theory.

change_log.change: Expanded the proposed demonstration with reproducibility, tolerances, loading conditions and practical coverage boundaries.
change_log.reason: These details make the innovation testable without presenting proposed criteria as published standards or finite validation as universality.

change_log.change: Used the supplied review's PDF-based findings while preserving landing-page, uncaptured-rendering and figure-extraction limitations.
change_log.reason: The record must distinguish the review's actual evidence access from unsupported implications of independent inspection.

change_log.change: Explained provisional relationships with every other supplied roster entry.
change_log.reason: Only their titles were provided; useful organizational distinctions can be retained as synthesis without asserting verified technical comparisons.

unresolved_issues: Whether work after February 2024 has resolved or materially narrowed any of the identified theoretical gaps is not established by the supplied record.
The universality class of the ductile-to-brittle transition, its finite-rate behavior and its large-system character remain unresolved in the supplied assessment.
The generality and practical consequences of continuum arguments linking stress overshoots to shear-banding instabilities require clarification across materials and loading conditions.
Operational preparation descriptors, quantitative prediction tolerances, observation times and a concrete withheld test set have not been specified.
Transfer to frictional particles, metallic glasses, coatings, geological materials and chemistry-based design requires separate evidence.
Detailed overlap with the other roster concepts cannot be verified from titles alone; the review's recommendation to check their full contents remains pending.
The ar5iv rendering was not captured, and figure images were not inspected in the supplied review. Figure-dependent conclusions would require further examination.
